title: The Scholarship of Maple Street
premise: Ines Whitlock, a nonbinary debate champion at Maplewood High, has survived by being unremarkable — until notes signed by the school's legendary ghost, 'The Cartographer,' begin appearing in their locker, each one naming a hidden truth about Maple Street itself: the town's founding fortune was built on a stolen Black-owned mapmaking business. As Ines investigates with the help of rival debater Theo and ghost-tour guide Marisol, the notes grow more personal, forcing Ines to confront their own family's complicity — and their own silence about who they are. The climax comes at prom, when Ines must choose between accepting a prestigious scholarship funded by the tainted fortune or publicly exposing the truth. They choose truth, reading the Cartographer's final note aloud, and discover the ghost is not dead at all but the elderly descendant of the erased cartographers, watching from the back of the gym.
about_author: F. M. Whitlock is the pen name of a former high-school debate coach who spent a decade listening to teenagers argue beautifully about things that didn't matter to them. They write young adult fiction about the arguments that do.

chapters.title: Head Down, Grades Up
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. We meet Ines mid-debate tournament, winning flawlessly while staying personally invisible; at home, they deflect their mother's questions about college plans and pronouns with practiced neutrality. The emotional beat is the exhaustion of performing a self that fits in every room except their own.

chapters.title: The Legend of the Cartographer
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. During her ghost-tour shift, Marisol recounts the Maplewood legend: a mapmaker who vanished in 1954, leaving behind maps of streets that don't exist. She notices fresh chalk marks on the tour route that match the old maps. The beat is curiosity sharpening into unease.

chapters.title: Note One
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. A note appears in Ines's locker: 'You win arguments you don't believe. Why?' The ink shimmers copper and won't smudge. Ines assumes a prank by debate rivals. The beat is a crack in the armor — someone has seen through the performance.

chapters.title: Impossible Ink
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo, Ines's chief rival, denies writing the note but is fascinated; together they test the ink, which resists every solvent and glows faintly under blacklight. The beat is reluctant alliance — two competitors united by a puzzle neither can claim.

chapters.title: What the Notes Know
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. A second note names Ines's grandmother's maiden name — a detail Ines has told no one. Fear sets in: this isn't a prank, it's surveillance, or something stranger. The beat is paranoia braided with an unwilling thrill at being truly known.

chapters.title: Maple Street, 1954
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Researching for her tours, Marisol finds the 1954 city directory lists a cartography shop on Maple Street owned by the Okafor family — absent from every later record. The beat is the first hard evidence that the town's cheerful history has a hole in it.

chapters.title: The Scholarship
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines is nominated for the Whitmore Scholarship — full ride, endowed by the family whose name is on half the town. Their mother is ecstatic; Ines feels oddly hollow. The beat is ambition colliding with instinct: something about the Whitmore name itches.

chapters.title: Rivals, Sort Of
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo admits the notes terrify him because he wants to be seen too — his perfect-student act hides a family falling apart. He and Ines agree to investigate together, officially. The beat is vulnerability traded like contraband.

chapters.title: The Basement Archive
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Following a note's riddle, the trio breaks into the library basement and finds a sealed box of Okafor maps — including one of Maple Street with houses drawn where the school now stands. The beat is wonder curdling into guilt: the school sits on something taken.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Silence
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines asks their grandmother about the Okafors; she goes pale and says only, 'Some maps are drawn so people get lost.' Later Ines finds her burning old letters. The beat is the discovery that inheritance includes secrets, not just money.

chapters.title: Labels
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. At a debate practice, a coach misgenders Ines repeatedly; Ines says nothing, and Theo watches them shrink. That night a new note reads: 'Say it once and the room changes shape.' The beat is anger at the world and tenderness toward the friend who won't claim themself.

chapters.title: Marisol's Theory
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol argues the Cartographer isn't supernatural — the ink matches a pigment formula from a 1950s art supply catalog, meaning someone alive is making these notes with period-accurate materials. The beat is the pivot from ghost story to mystery.

chapters.title: The Whitmore Wing
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Invited to a scholarship donor dinner, Ines tours the Whitmore estate and spots a framed Okafor map labeled as a 'Whitmore original.' The theft is no longer abstract. The beat is quiet fury — justice has a price tag and Ines is being bought.

chapters.title: Prom Committee Politics
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Prom approaches as a pressure cooker: Theo is running for prom king to please his father, Ines refuses every gendered category on the ballot form. A note appears taped to the ballot box: 'Why are there boxes at all?' The beat is public friction becoming private courage.

chapters.title: Caught
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines is caught breaking into the archive again and suspended, jeopardizing the scholarship. Their mother's disappointment cuts deeper than the school's punishment. The beat is rock bottom — the cost of truth arriving all at once.

chapters.title: The Letters Under the Floor
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol decodes a map's marginalia and finds correspondence proving the Whitmores forged debt documents to seize the Okafor shop in 1954. She brings it to Ines's window at midnight. The beat is evidence as a torch passed hand to hand.

chapters.title: Who Writes the Notes
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Following the ink trail, Ines finds the supply source: a shuttered stationer's still occupied by an old man — Mr. Okafor's son, alive, elderly, and the author of every note. He never died; he was erased. The beat is revelation replacing haunting: the ghost is a witness.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The Whitmore foundation, tipped off about Ines's 'investigations,' offers to fast-track the scholarship if Ines signs an NDA regarding 'historical materials.' Accepting means silence; refusing means nothing. The beat is temptation rendered precisely, without villains twirling mustaches.

chapters.title: The Argument at Home
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines finally tells their mother everything — the notes, the theft, and their own name and pronouns — in one breathless confession. It goes badly, then, hours later, quietly well: her grandmother's letters surface, revealing she once tried to testify for the Okafors. The beat is generational courage finally spoken aloud.

chapters.title: Prom Night
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. At prom, Ines takes the microphone during the scholarship presentation and reads the Okafor letters aloud as Theo live-streams and Marisol guards the door. The gym freezes; the Whitmore representative moves to cut the sound. The beat is terror transfigured into voice — the debate champion finally arguing something they believe.

chapters.title: After the Applause
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Fallout: the district opens an inquiry, Theo loses the crown and gains his father's grudging respect, and Mr. Okafor is invited to address the school board. Ines loses the scholarship and doesn't regret it. The beat is the strange lightness of consequences honestly earned.

chapters.title: A New Map
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Graduation week: Mr. Okafor gives Ines the original Maple Street map, blank on one side. 'Draw what comes next,' he says. Ines writes their full name in the corner — in ordinary, smudgeable ink. The beat is identity claimed not as revelation but as authorship.
